Psalms 101.audience: A psalm of David in which the king vows to rule his house and land with integrity.

culture.title: Morning justice
culture.text: "I will early destroy all the wicked of the land"—kings and judges heard cases in the morning at the gate (Jeremiah 21:12).

culture.title: Choosing servants
culture.text: The king will choose faithful servants and remove deceivers from his household—the officials who served at court.

Psalms 102.audience: Titled "A Prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed." It is one of the church's Penitential Psalms. Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes verses 25–27 of the Son.

culture.title: A pelican in the wilderness
culture.text: The pelican, the owl of the desert, and a sparrow alone on the housetop are pictures of loneliness and desolation.

culture.title: Ashes like bread
culture.text: Mourners sat in ashes and put dust on their heads; the psalmist says he has "eaten ashes like bread."

culture.title: Garments wearing out
culture.text: Clothing wore out and was changed. Heaven and earth will wear out like a garment, but God remains.

Psalms 103.audience: A psalm of David calling his own soul to bless the LORD. It quotes God's self-description in Exodus 34:6 (Psalm 103:8).

culture.title: As far as east from west
culture.text: East and west—sunrise and sunset—are the farthest apart anything can be.

culture.title: Youth renewed like the eagle
culture.text: The eagle's strength and long life made it a picture of vigor (Isaiah 40:31).

culture.title: Grass and flowers
culture.text: Wildflowers bloom after the spring rains and wither when the hot desert wind passes over them.

Psalms 104.audience: Psalm 104 has no title. It praises God for creation and sustaining every creature. An Egyptian hymn to the sun god Aten has some similar themes, though this psalm addresses the LORD as creator of the sun.

culture.title: Storks in the fir trees
culture.text: Storks migrate through Israel in great numbers each spring and autumn; some nest in tall trees.

culture.title: Conies in the rocks
culture.text: The coney is the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks and cliffs, as around Engedi.

culture.title: Wine, oil, and bread
culture.text: Wine, olive oil, and bread were the three staples of daily life in the land.

Psalms 105.audience: Psalm 105 has no title. Its first fifteen verses appear in the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:8–22). It retells Israel's history from Abraham to the conquest.

culture.title: Joseph's fetters
culture.text: "Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron"—a detail of Joseph's imprisonment not given in Genesis.

culture.title: The land of Ham
culture.text: "The land of Ham" is a poetic name for Egypt, whose people were traced to Ham (Genesis 10:6).

Psalms 106.audience: Psalm 106 has no title. It confesses Israel's sins from Egypt to the exile and prays, "gather us from among the heathen" (Psalm 106:47). It ends Book IV with a doxology.

culture.title: Baalpeor and the dead
culture.text: Israel "ate the sacrifices of the dead" at Baalpeor (Numbers 25)—offerings to lifeless gods or for the dead.

culture.title: Sacrificing children to idols
culture.text: Israel sacrificed sons and daughters to the idols of Canaan, a practice condemned by the prophets (Jeremiah 7:31).

Psalms 107.audience: Psalm 107 opens Book V. It calls those the LORD has redeemed and "gathered... out of the lands, from the east, and from the west" (Psalm 107:3) to give thanks.

culture.title: Four kinds of rescue
culture.text: The psalm describes travelers lost in the desert, prisoners, the sick, and sailors in a storm—each crying out and being rescued.

culture.title: Merchants at sea
culture.text: "They that go down to the sea in ships"—sea trade was dominated by Phoenicians; Israelites knew the sea as dangerous.

Psalms 108.audience: A song of David combining Psalm 57:7–11 and Psalm 60:5–12.

culture.title: Psaltery and harp at dawn
culture.text: "Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early"—praise at daybreak with stringed instruments.

Psalms 109.audience: A psalm of David praying against a false accuser. Peter applied verse 8 to Judas: "his bishoprick let another take" (Acts 1:20).

culture.title: An accuser at the right hand
culture.text: In court, an accuser stood at the right hand of the accused (Zechariah 3:1).

culture.title: Children as beggars
culture.text: Without land or family support, orphans had to beg and "seek their bread also out of their desolate places."

Psalms 110.audience: A psalm of David. It is one of the Old Testament passages most often quoted in the New Testament; Jesus asked how David could call his son "Lord" (Matthew 22:43–45), and Hebrews builds on verse 4 (Hebrews 5–7).

culture.title: At the right hand
culture.text: Sitting at a king's right hand was the place of highest honor and authority (1 Kings 2:19).

culture.title: Enemies as a footstool
culture.text: Egyptian kings were depicted with their feet resting on images of defeated enemies.

culture.title: Melchizedek
culture.text: Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18). The psalm joins king and priest in one person.

Psalms 111.audience: Psalm 111 begins "Praise ye the LORD" (Hallelujah) and is an acrostic, each half-verse beginning with the next Hebrew letter. It pairs with Psalm 112.

culture.title: Remembering wonderful works
culture.text: "He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered"—Israel's feasts recalled God's acts in history.

Psalms 112.audience: Psalm 112 is an acrostic like Psalm 111 and describes the blessings of the person who fears the LORD. Paul quotes verse 9 in 2 Corinthians 9:9.

culture.title: Lending graciously
culture.text: Lending to the poor without interest was commanded in the law (Leviticus 25:35–37).

culture.title: A horn exalted
culture.text: "His horn shall be exalted with honour"—the horn as a sign of strength and dignity.

Psalms 113.audience: Psalms 113–118 form the Egyptian Hallel, sung at Passover and other feasts in later Jewish practice. The hymn Jesus and his disciples sang after the Last Supper was likely from these psalms (Matthew 26:30).

culture.title: Raised from the dunghill
culture.text: The poor and outcasts sat at the town's rubbish heap. God lifts them to sit with princes (compare 1 Samuel 2:8).

culture.title: The barren woman
culture.text: Childlessness brought shame and insecurity to a woman in the ancient world.

Psalms 114.audience: Psalm 114 recalls the exodus, the crossing of the sea and the Jordan, and water from the rock. It is part of the Hallel sung at Passover.

culture.title: A strange language
culture.text: Israel left "a people of strange language"—Egyptian, unlike their own.

culture.title: Mountains skipping
culture.text: Mountains skipping like rams and hills like lambs describe the earthquake at Sinai (Exodus 19:18).

Psalms 115.audience: Psalm 115 contrasts the living God with idols. It calls Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD to trust him (Psalm 115:9–11).

culture.title: Idols of silver and gold
culture.text: Idols were carved of wood and overlaid with silver and gold, with mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands, and feet that could not work.

culture.title: The dead in silence
culture.text: "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence"—Sheol was thought of as a place of silence.

Psalms 116.audience: Psalm 116 has no title. It gives thanks for rescue from death and promises to pay vows "in the presence of all his people" (Psalm 116:14).

culture.title: The cup of salvation
culture.text: A cup of wine was lifted at thanksgiving meals. Jewish Passover practice includes four cups of wine.

culture.title: Paying vows in the courts
culture.text: Vows were paid with offerings at the temple in Jerusalem, in front of the congregation.

Psalms 117.audience: Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm and the shortest chapter in the Bible, two verses long. Paul quotes verse 1 to show that the Gentiles praise God (Romans 15:11).

culture.title: All nations
culture.text: The psalm calls "all ye nations" and "all ye people" to praise the LORD.

Psalms 118.audience: Psalm 118 closes the Egyptian Hallel. The crowds shouted verse 26 when Jesus entered Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9), and Jesus quoted verse 22 about himself (Matthew 21:42).

culture.title: The head stone of the corner
culture.text: A cornerstone joined two walls and held the building together. A stone rejected by builders becomes the most important one.

culture.title: Binding the sacrifice
culture.text: "Bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar"—a festal procession to the altar.

culture.title: Gates of righteousness
culture.text: Worshippers asked to enter the temple gates, as in Psalms 15 and 24.

Psalms 119.audience: Psalm 119 is the longest psalm and longest chapter in the Bible, with 176 verses. It is an acrostic of 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, each with eight verses beginning with that letter.

culture.title: The Hebrew letters
culture.text: The KJV prints the name of each Hebrew letter (Aleph, Beth, Gimel, and so on) above its stanza.

culture.title: A bottle in the smoke
culture.text: A leather wineskin hung in a smoky house became dried, blackened, and cracked.

culture.title: A lamp to the feet
culture.text: Small clay oil lamps gave just enough light to see the next step on a dark path.

Psalms 120.audience: Psalm 120 is the first of fifteen psalms titled A Song of degrees (Psalms 120–134), ‘songs of ascents,’, probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.

culture.title: Meshech and Kedar
culture.text: Meshech was a people far to the north in Asia Minor and Kedar an Arabian tribe to the southeast—distant, warlike peoples.

culture.title: Coals of juniper
culture.text: The roots of the broom tree ("juniper") make charcoal that burns very hot and long.

Psalms 121.audience: A Song of degrees for pilgrims on the road: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills" (Psalm 121:1). Jerusalem lies in the hills.

culture.title: Sun by day, moon by night
culture.text: Travelers faced sunstroke by day. Some ancient peoples also feared harm from the moon.

culture.title: A keeper who does not sleep
culture.text: Watchmen guarded cities and flocks at night. God is a keeper who "shall neither slumber nor sleep."

Psalms 122.audience: A Song of degrees of David celebrating arrival in Jerusalem: "Our feet shall stand within thy gates" (Psalm 122:2).

culture.title: A city compact together
culture.text: Jerusalem was a walled city with houses built closely together.

culture.title: Thrones of judgment
culture.text: Jerusalem was the seat of David's house and the place where the king judged cases.

Psalms 123.audience: A short Song of degrees asking for mercy from those who have endured contempt.

culture.title: Eyes on the master's hand
culture.text: Servants watched their master's hand for signals and provision, as a maid watched her mistress.

Psalms 124.audience: A Song of degrees of David giving thanks that "the LORD... was on our side" when enemies rose up.

culture.title: A bird escaped from the snare
culture.text: Bird catchers used snares and nets. A broken snare lets the bird escape.

culture.title: Flash floods
culture.text: Sudden rains could turn dry wadis into raging torrents that swept everything away.

Psalms 125.audience: A Song of degrees comparing those who trust the LORD to Mount Zion, which cannot be moved.

culture.title: Mountains round about Jerusalem
culture.text: Jerusalem is surrounded by higher hills—the Mount of Olives to the east and ridges to the south and west.

culture.title: The rod of the wicked
culture.text: The rod (sceptre) of foreign rule will not rest on the land allotted to the righteous.

Psalms 126.audience: A Song of degrees celebrating the return "when the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion" (Psalm 126:1).

culture.title: Streams in the south
culture.text: The south (Negev) is dry, but winter rains suddenly fill its streambeds with water.

culture.title: Sowing in tears
culture.text: Sowing seed in hard times meant hoping for a harvest that was not certain. Reaping brought shouts of joy.

Psalms 127.audience: A Song of degrees for Solomon. It says that work, building, and family are vain without the LORD.

culture.title: Watchmen on the walls
culture.text: City watchmen guarded the walls at night against attackers and thieves.

culture.title: Arrows in a quiver
culture.text: Sons were a family's strength and defenders. A man with many sons would "speak with the enemies in the gate" without fear.

Psalms 128.audience: A Song of degrees blessing the family of the one who fears the LORD.

culture.title: A fruitful vine and olive plants
culture.text: Vines grew against house walls, and young olive shoots sprang up around an old tree—pictures of a wife and children in a household.

Psalms 129.audience: A Song of degrees in which Israel recalls being afflicted "from my youth" but not defeated.

culture.title: Plowing on the back
culture.text: "The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows"—a picture of brutal oppression, like whip marks.

culture.title: Grass on the housetops
culture.text: Seeds sprouted on flat earthen roofs but withered quickly in the shallow soil.

Psalms 130.audience: A Song of degrees and one of the church's Penitential Psalms: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee" (Psalm 130:1).

culture.title: Watchmen waiting for morning
culture.text: Night watchmen waited for daybreak to end their watch. The psalmist waits for God more than they wait for morning.

Psalms 131.audience: A short Song of degrees of David expressing quiet trust.

culture.title: A weaned child
culture.text: Children were weaned at around two or three years old. A weaned child rests with its mother without demanding to nurse.

Psalms 132.audience: A Song of degrees recalling David's oath to find a place for the ark and God's oath to David's line. Solomon quotes verses 8–10 at the temple dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41–42).

culture.title: Ephratah and the fields of the wood
culture.text: Ephratah is Bethlehem, David's hometown, and "the fields of the wood" Kirjath-jearim, where the ark had stayed (1 Samuel 7:1–2).

culture.title: Priests clothed with righteousness
culture.text: Priests wore special garments for service. The psalm prays they be clothed with righteousness and salvation.

Psalms 133.audience: A Song of degrees of David celebrating brothers dwelling together in unity.

culture.title: Oil on Aaron's beard
culture.text: At Aaron's ordination, oil was poured on his head (Leviticus 8:12). The image is of abundant blessing flowing down.

culture.title: The dew of Hermon
culture.text: Mount Hermon in the north receives heavy dew, which waters plants in the dry summer.

Psalms 134.audience: The last Song of degrees, addressed to "all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD" (Psalm 134:1)—the Levites on night duty in the temple.

culture.title: Night service in the temple
culture.text: Levites served in the temple day and night (1 Chronicles 9:33), guarding it and leading praise.

Psalms 135.audience: Psalm 135 calls the servants of the LORD in his house to praise him, recalling the exodus and the defeat of Sihon and Og.

culture.title: Wind from the treasuries
culture.text: God "bringeth the wind out of his treasuries"—wind and rain pictured as stored and released by God (Job 38:22).

culture.title: Idols repeated
culture.text: The description of idols with mouths and eyes that do not work repeats Psalm 115:4–8.

Psalms 136.audience: Every one of its 26 verses ends with the refrain "for his mercy endureth for ever," probably sung by the congregation in response to a leader (Ezra 3:11). Jewish tradition calls it the Great Hallel.

culture.title: Responsive singing
culture.text: A leader sang each line and the people answered with the refrain—a pattern of worship also seen at the temple dedication (2 Chronicles 7:3).

Psalms 137.audience: Psalm 137 was written by exiles in Babylon who remembered Zion. Readers who had lived through the exile knew its grief and anger firsthand.

culture.title: Rivers of Babylon
culture.text: Babylon lay on the Euphrates, with a network of irrigation canals. Exiles were settled by such waterways, like the river Chebar (Ezekiel 1:1).

culture.title: Harps on the willows
culture.text: The exiles hung their harps on the trees—refusing to play songs of Zion for their captors.

culture.title: Edom's taunt
culture.text: Edom cheered Jerusalem's destruction: "Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation" (compare Obadiah 1:11–14).

Psalms 138.audience: A psalm of David giving thanks "before the gods" (Psalm 138:1) and promising that the kings of the earth will praise the LORD.

culture.title: Worshipping toward the temple
culture.text: Worshippers bowed toward the temple when praying (1 Kings 8:29–30).

Psalms 139.audience: A psalm of David on God's knowledge of every part of a person's life, from before birth.

culture.title: Wings of the morning
culture.text: "The wings of the morning" is the dawn in the east; "the uttermost parts of the sea" is the far west—the extremes of the known world.

culture.title: Formed in the womb
culture.text: Being "curiously wrought" uses a word for embroidery or weaving—the body's formation pictured as skilled handwork.

Psalms 140.audience: A psalm of David asking deliverance from violent and slanderous men. Paul quotes verse 3 in Romans 3:13.

culture.title: Adders' poison
culture.text: "Adders' poison is under their lips"—venomous snakes as a picture of harmful speech.

culture.title: Covering the head in battle
culture.text: "Thou hast covered my head in the day of battle"—God as a helmet.

Psalms 141.audience: A psalm of David asking that his prayer be "set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice" (Psalm 141:2).

culture.title: Incense and the evening sacrifice
culture.text: Incense was burned on the golden altar every evening as the lamps were lit (Exodus 30:8), and the evening lamb was offered.

culture.title: A watch on the mouth
culture.text: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips"—like a guard at a city gate.

Psalms 142.audience: Titled "Maschil of David; A Prayer when he was in the cave" (1 Samuel 22:1 or 24:3).

culture.title: No refuge
culture.text: "There was no man that would know me: refuge failed me." A fugitive depended on others for shelter and food.

Psalms 143.audience: A psalm of David and the last of the church's seven Penitential Psalms. Paul echoes verse 2, "in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16).

culture.title: A thirsty land
culture.text: "My soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land"—dry, cracked ground in late summer before the autumn rains.

Psalms 144.audience: A psalm of David drawing on Psalm 18 and Psalm 8. It prays for victory and for a prosperous people.

culture.title: Corner stones of a palace
culture.text: Daughters are compared to carved corner pillars of a palace—strong and beautiful.

culture.title: Full garners
culture.text: Storehouses full of grain and fields full of sheep describe a prosperous land.

Psalms 145.audience: Titled "David's Psalm of praise." It is an acrostic; the standard Hebrew text lacks a line for the letter nun, but a Dead Sea Scrolls copy and the Greek translation include it.

culture.title: God as king
culture.text: "I will extol thee, my God, O king"—God's kingdom is "an everlasting kingdom" (Psalm 145:13).

culture.title: Eyes waiting on God
culture.text: "The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season"—a verse used in later Jewish table prayers.

Psalms 146.audience: Psalms 146–150 each begin and end with "Praise ye the LORD" (Hallelujah), forming the closing praise of the book.

culture.title: Trusting princes
culture.text: "Put not your trust in princes"—rulers die and their plans perish with them.

culture.title: Care for the vulnerable
culture.text: God preserves the strangers and relieves the fatherless and widow—those the law commanded Israel to protect.

Psalms 147.audience: Psalm 147 praises God who "doth build up Jerusalem" and "gathereth together the outcasts of Israel" (Psalm 147:2).

culture.title: Naming the stars
culture.text: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names."

culture.title: Snow and hail
culture.text: Snow "like wool," frost "like ashes," and hail "like morsels" describe winter weather in the hills of Jerusalem.

Psalms 148.audience: Psalm 148 calls all creation to praise—angels, sun, moon, stars, sea creatures, weather, mountains, animals, kings, and people of every age.

culture.title: Dragons and deeps
culture.text: "Dragons" here are great sea creatures (Genesis 1:21). Even they are called to praise God.

Psalms 149.audience: Psalm 149 calls Israel to praise with dance, timbrel, and harp, holding "a twoedged sword in their hand" (Psalm 149:6).

culture.title: Dance and timbrel
culture.text: Dancing with timbrels (hand drums) was part of celebration and worship (Exodus 15:20).

culture.title: Kings in chains
culture.text: Binding captured kings with chains and nobles with fetters was the practice of victorious armies.

Psalms 150.audience: Psalm 150 closes the book of Psalms, calling everything that has breath to praise the LORD.

culture.title: Temple instruments
culture.text: The psalm names the trumpet (shofar), psaltery, harp, timbrel, stringed instruments, organs (pipes), and loud and high-sounding cymbals—the full range of instruments known in Israel.
